children: The Tata Sons dispute is more than a leadership battle. It tests whether a chairman’s casting vote can override rights reserved for Tata Trusts’ nominee directors, even as regulatory pressure and governance constraints complicate the path ahead.
I. The Boardroom War Has Become an Indian Institution

For a market that once prided itself on promoter consensus and quiet settlement over dinner at the club, India has developed a remarkable appetite for public corporate combat. In the last decade alone we have watched the Tatas and the Mistrys litigate all the way to the Supreme Court; the Infosys founders take on their own board in the pages of the financial press; Invesco try to force an extraordinary general meeting on a resisting Zee board; the Burmans prise control of Religare from an entrenched executive chairperson; Valli Arunachalam take the Murugappa family holding company to the Tribunal; and, this year, the Jagran promoter family carry its quarrel into the National Company Law Tribunal.

The pattern beneath these disputes is consistent, and it is worth naming precisely, because it is the key to the Tata affair as well. Indian corporate control is almost never held through equity alone. It is held through a lattice of
control instruments

— affirmative vote rights embedded in articles, nominee directorships, trust deeds, quorum clauses, family settlements, casting votes. These instruments work perfectly for as long as everyone inside the tent agrees. The moment consensus fails, the instruments turn out to have been drafted for a world in which the question now being asked was never expected to arise. Litigation is what happens when a control document meets a contingency its draftsman did not imagine.
That is exactly where Tata Sons finds itself today.
II. What Happened at Bombay House

On 17 September 2026, the board of Tata Sons Private Limited passed two resolutions. The first granted N. Chandrasekaran a fresh five-year term as Executive Chairman, his current term running to 20 February 2027. The second set in motion steps towards compliance with the Reserve Bank of India’s listing mandate.

Both resolutions carried 4–1. The single dissent on each came from Noel Tata, Chairman of the Tata Trusts and one of the Trusts’ two nominee directors on the Tata Sons board. The other Trusts nominee, Venu Srinivasan, voted with the majority — alongside Saurabh Agrawal and the independent directors Harish Manwani and Anita Marangoly George.
Two features make this more than an ordinary split vote.

First, on 12 August 2026 Mr. Chandrasekaran had publicly indicated he would not seek reappointment. The board’s request that he reconsider, and his acceptance, came barely five weeks later — a reversal the Trusts have described as premature.

Second, and decisively, Tata Sons’ Articles of Association contain a reserved-matters architecture. Article 121, read with Article 104B, requires that specified board decisions carry the affirmative vote of a majority of the directors nominated by the Tata Trusts. With exactly two such nominees on the board, and those two split one against one, the Trusts’ position is stark: no majority of nominee directors affirmed anything, and the resolution is therefore
void ab initio

. The board’s position, fortified by opinions from senior counsel Sudipto Sarkar and Justice B. N. Srikrishna (Retd.), is that a deadlock among the nominees is a tie, and a tie is what the Chairman’s casting vote exists to break.
The Trusts have engaged Dr. Abhishek Manu Singhvi. Nobody engages Dr. Singhvi to write a letter.
III. The Legal Question at the Centre of It All

Strip away the personalities and the dispute reduces to a single question of construction: can a general casting-vote provision operate inside a space that the articles have specifically reserved to a defined class of directors?
The competing readings
The board’s reading is sequential — call it the
if/then
construction. Article 121 asks whether the nominees approved; the nominees divided; a division is an equality of votes; the Chairman breaks it; the resolution passes.
The Trusts’ reading is cumulative — the
double-barrel
construction. Article 121 imposes two independent conditions: an overall board majority
and

an affirmative majority of the Trusts’ nominees. Failure of the second is not a tie to be broken but a condition precedent that has simply not been satisfied. On this reading there is no deadlock at all; there is a defeated resolution.
Why the Trusts have the better of the construction argument
Three reasons, in my assessment.
One: the canon of generalia specialibus non derogant

Where a general provision and a specific provision occupy the same field, the specific governs. A casting vote is the most general of board mechanics. A reserved-matter veto is the most specific of protections. To let the former consume the latter is to read the protection out of the document.

Two: the purposive test. Why does Article 121 exist? It exists so that a 66 per cent owner which does not manage the company can nonetheless ensure that certain decisions — the identity of the Chairman chief among them — cannot be taken over its objection. If a single defecting nominee converts that protection into a tie which a non-nominee then resolves, the protection is not merely weakened; it is inverted. The clause becomes a mechanism by which the board appoints its own Chairman over the owner’s objection. No draftsman intends that.

Three: the casting vote was exercised by someone other than a participant in the deadlock. Under Article 68(ii) of Table F, Schedule I to the Companies Act, 2013, the casting vote is a device of the chair of that meeting, resolving equality among those who voted. Here the tie was between two nominee directors; the vote that broke it came from elsewhere entirely. That is a structurally unusual result, and unusual results in construction are usually a signal that the construction is wrong.
The interested-director problem

There is a further difficulty the board will have to answer. A Chairman presiding over — and, on the board’s own case, benefiting from the deciding vote on — the resolution extending his own tenure raises immediate questions under Section 184 of the Companies Act, 2013 and under the Secretarial Standard on Meetings of the Board of Directors (SS-1), which contemplates that a director concerned or interested in a matter should neither participate nor vote.
Section 184(2) applies in terms to contracts and arrangements; whether a reappointment resolution falls squarely within it is arguable. But the
principle
of disinterested decision-making does not depend on the section fitting neatly. In
Dale & Carrington Invt. (P) Ltd. v. P. K. Prathapan
, (2005) 1 SCC 212, the Supreme Court was unsparing about directors who exercise fiduciary power in their own favour. That reasoning will be pressed, and it will not be comfortable to answer.
Where the board is on stronger ground

Two points genuinely favour Tata Sons. First, the “change of heart” argument is weak in law. An announced intention not to seek reappointment is not a resignation; nothing in the Act or in general principle prevents a director from revisiting a stated intention before any operative date. Public reliance is a reputational point, not a legal one. Second, the board acted on contemporaneous written opinions from eminent counsel. That does not make the resolution valid, but it substantially blunts any allegation of
mala fides
— which matters enormously if this reaches Sections 241 and 242.
IV. The Second Front: The Reserve Bank
The leadership dispute is entangled with a regulatory one, and the regulatory one has a harder edge.

Tata Sons was placed in the Upper Layer of the RBI’s Scale Based Regulation framework on 30 September 2022, carrying with it a mandatory listing obligation within three years. That deadline passed in September 2025. Tata Sons’ application to surrender its Core Investment Company registration — the route by which it hoped to exit the obligation altogether — was rejected by the RBI on 11 September 2026. The regulator has since lodged a caveat in the Bombay High Court, ensuring it will be heard before any interim order touching the listing mandate.

This is the most under-appreciated element of the whole affair. The RBI is not a bystander. Section 45-IE of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 empowers the Bank to supersede the board of a non-banking financial company in the public interest or in the interest of the company itself. Nobody expects that outcome. But its existence changes the negotiating temperature in a way that a purely private dispute never could. A prolonged shareholder deadlock that leaves a systemically important NBFC in continuing breach of a listing direction is not a stable position for either faction.

And the listing question cuts across the leadership question in an awkward way. A listing requires a special resolution — 75 per cent of votes cast. The Trusts hold roughly 65.9 per cent. On paper they can block it. But whether they can
cast
those votes is the subject of the third front.
V. The Third Front: A Shareholder That Cannot Meet
Here the dispute leaves company law altogether.

The Tata Trusts are public charitable trusts governed by the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950. Sir Dorabji Tata Trust holds approximately 28 per cent of Tata Sons; Sir Ratan Tata Trust approximately 23.6 per cent. The Charity Commissioner has initiated an inquiry into SRTT’s trustee composition, specifically its compliance with the statutory cap on life trustees introduced by the 2025 amendment. Pending that inquiry, SRTT has been unable to convene a board meeting.
A trust that cannot meet cannot resolve. A trust that cannot resolve cannot authorise its representative. And under Article 86 of Tata Sons’ Articles, the two principal trusts must
jointly

nominate the representative whose presence is required for quorum at the general meeting. The consequence has already materialised: a Tata Sons general meeting stood adjourned for want of quorum — by all accounts the first such occurrence in the company’s history. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has extended the annual general meeting deadline to 18 November 2026.

This is an extraordinary state of affairs. A regulatory proceeding against a charity has, in effect, disenfranchised a 23.6 per cent shareholder of India’s most significant holding company and paralysed its general meeting. Whatever else it demonstrates, it demonstrates that the Tata governance architecture has a single point of failure nobody stress-tested.
VI. The Options Open to Noel Tata
The shareholder route — the strongest card
The board has voted. The owners have not. That distinction is the whole game.

Under Section 100 of the Companies Act, 2013, members holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights may requisition an extraordinary general meeting. Under Section 169, read with the special notice requirement in Section 115, a director may be removed by ordinary resolution before the expiry of his term, subject to a reasonable opportunity of being heard. A Chairman who ceases to be a director cannot continue as Chairman. This is the shortest route from grievance to result, and it does not require anyone to win an argument about Article 121.
The law here is settled and favourable. In
Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Escorts Ltd.

, (1986) 1 SCC 264, the Supreme Court held that a shareholder exercising its statutory right to requisition a meeting and move for removal of directors need not disclose its reasons, and that its motives are not justiciable.
In
Invesco Developing Markets Fund v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd.

(Bombay High Court, Division Bench, judgment dated 22 March 2022), the Court set aside an injunction restraining a requisitioned extraordinary general meeting, holding that a board cannot pre-judge the legality of resolutions that shareholders propose to move. Taken together, these authorities mean a board has very little room to obstruct a properly requisitioned meeting.

The obstacle, therefore, is not legal. It is arithmetical and procedural — the SRTT freeze and the Article 86 joint-nomination requirement. Resolve those, and the shareholder route is close to unanswerable. Fail to resolve them, and it is unavailable.
Sections 241 and 242 — powerful but double-edged

A petition before the National Company Law Tribunal alleging conduct prejudicial to the interests of a member is the classic vehicle. Section 242(2) gives the Tribunal expansive relief, including regulating the conduct of the company’s affairs and setting aside transactions.
But counsel will have to reckon honestly with
Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. Cyrus Investments (P) Ltd.

, (2021) 9 SCC 449. The Supreme Court there set aside the NCLAT’s order reinstating Cyrus Mistry, upheld the validity of the very affirmative-vote architecture now in issue as a legitimate protection rather than an oppressive device, and made clear that removal of a person from executive office — even in a manner some may find ungracious — does not without more amount to oppression. The bar set by
Shanti Prasad Jain v. Kalinga Tubes Ltd.
, AIR 1965 SC 1535, and
Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
, (1981) 3 SCC 333 — conduct that is burdensome, harsh and wrongful, and a visible lack of probity — remains a high one.
There is, however, a real irony the Trusts can exploit. The 2021 judgment is the strongest available authority for the proposition that these articles are
valid and enforceable
. A board now arguing that a general casting vote overrides them is, in a sense, arguing against the very reasoning that saved Tata Sons in 2021.
Declaratory relief and the forum question

Reports suggest the Trusts may move the Supreme Court. With respect, that would be an unusual first step. Neither Article 32 nor Article 136 of the Constitution naturally accommodates a first-instance dispute about the construction of a private company’s articles. The realistic fora are the National Company Law Tribunal under Sections 241–242, or the Bombay High Court on its original side for a declaration that the resolution is void. Even then, Section 430 bars civil courts from determining matters the Tribunal is empowered to decide — a bar the Supreme Court applied firmly in
Shashi Prakash Khemka v. NEPC Micon Ltd.
, (2019) 18 SCC 569. Expect a jurisdictional skirmish before anyone reaches the merits.
Board-level leverage

Least dramatic, possibly most effective. If Article 121 means what the Trusts say it means, then every reserved matter — reportedly including investments above ₹100 crore — requires the same affirmative majority. A nominee who withholds consent across the reserved list can make the company very difficult to run, without filing a single pleading. It is a blunt instrument and carries its own fiduciary risks. It is also, in practice, the fastest route to a negotiated outcome.
VII. The Options Open to Chandrasekaran and the Board

Ratify at the general meeting. If the annual general meeting can be convened and the resolution placed before members, a shareholder endorsement cures a great deal. This, of course, depends on arithmetic the board may not control.
Stand on the opinions. Contemporaneous advice from Sudipto Sarkar and Justice Srikrishna is a formidable answer to any allegation of bad faith, and bad faith is the engine of a Section 241 petition.
Let the regulator carry the argument. The board’s listing resolution has the Reserve Bank behind it. Opposing a mandatory regulatory direction is a difficult posture to maintain in open court.

Section 98. Where it is impracticable to call a meeting in the manner prescribed, the Tribunal may order one to be called and give directions — including on quorum. If the SRTT freeze continues to block the annual general meeting, an application under Section 98 is an obvious move, and one that would neatly sidestep Article 86.
VIII. The Questions Nobody Can Yet Answer
Honesty requires flagging what is genuinely unsettled. There is no Supreme Court authority directly deciding whether a chairman’s casting vote can operate within a reserved-matter veto.
Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. v. Cyrus Investments (P) Ltd.
upheld the validity of such articles; it did not decide what happens when the protected class deadlocks internally.
World Phone India Pvt. Ltd. v. WPI Group Inc., USA
(Delhi High Court, judgment dated 15 March 2013) and
V. B. Rangaraj v. V. B. Gopalakrishnan

, (1992) 1 SCC 160, establish that affirmative rights must live in the articles to bind the company — they say nothing about how those rights behave under strain. This is, so far as I can see, a question of first impression in India.
IX. What to Watch
Four things, in order of consequence.
The annual general meeting, on or before 18 November 2026. Whether it is convened at all, and on what quorum, will decide more than any pleading.
The Charity Commissioner’s inquiry into Sir Ratan Tata Trust. Until that shareholder can meet, no faction controls the outcome. This is the true chokepoint.
The Reserve Bank’s posture. If the Bank signals impatience with continued non-compliance, the leadership dispute will be resolved by external pressure rather than internal argument.

The Shapoorji Pallonji Group. Holding roughly 18.4 per cent, under real refinancing pressure, and materially better off with a listing than a buyback given the post-April 2026 tax differential, the SP Group is the swing interest that both factions have every reason to court.
X. The Lesson for Every Indian Board

Two decades of drafting control architecture has taught Indian promoters and their advisers to protect against hostility from outside. The Tata dispute is a reminder that the greater danger is disagreement from within — and that reserved-matter clauses drafted on the assumption of a unified nominee bloc will fail precisely when they are most needed.

Three drafting lessons follow, and I would urge every general counsel of a holding company to apply them this quarter. Provide expressly for deadlock within a protected class — escalation, referral to shareholders, a deciding nominee, anything but silence. Never leave quorum dependent on the internal functioning of an entity you do not control. And subject your governance documents to genuine stress-testing: not “does this work when we agree”, but “what does this document say on the worst day of our corporate life”.

Tata Sons is not in crisis because anybody behaved dishonourably. It is in crisis because a superbly drafted set of articles met a contingency it did not contemplate, at the precise moment a regulator ran out of patience and a charity regulator froze a shareholder. That combination was improbable. It was not unforeseeable.
Corporate India will be reading the eventual judgment very closely indeed — and, I suspect, redrafting a great many articles of association on the strength of it.
